South Korea Stock Market Crash: KOSPI plunges over 8% amid tech sell-off; Samsung, SK Hynix tumble
sum: South Korea Stock Market Crash: South Korea's benchmark stock index, the KOSPI, plunged over 8 per cent on Thursday, November 5, triggering a circuit breaker as heavyweight stocks Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix tumbled amid a sharp sell-off in global technology stocks.

As of 6:10 am, the KOSPI was trading 6.5 per cent lower, down 364.24 points at 5,019.56. Earlier in the session, the index had slumped to an intraday low of 4,911.28, marking a decline of 8.8 per cent from the previous close of 5,383.80.
The sharp decline in South Korea's stock market came amid concerns over AI data-centre investments, a sell-off in US semiconductor stocks and weakness in the country's major chipmakers.

AI data-centre concerns: Investors are concerned that the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could lead to tighter regulations on data centres and power consumption. This could delay new AI infrastructure projects and reduce future demand for chips.

US semiconductor sell-off: The decline in US chip stocks spilled over into South Korea's export- and semiconductor-heavy market. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) slipped around 10 per cent, marking its worst performance since March 2020.
Samsung and SK Hynix weakness: Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the KOSPI's heavyweight constituents, led the decline.

Samsung Electronics shares were trading around 7 per cent lower at 1,87,200. The stock had touched an intraday low of 1,79,200, reflecting a decline of over 11 per cent from its previous close of 2,01,500.

Samsung Electronics stock expands long-term memory deals as AI demand surges
sum: Samsung Electronics is expanding long-term memory supply agreements as customers seek to secure chips for the next several years, Korea JoongAng Daily reported on Monday, November 2, 2026. The agreements respond to tight memory markets driven by artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

Samsung said during its third-quarter earnings conference call on October 29 that it had signed long-term contracts with 10 customers and was negotiating with another 10. Demand is spreading beyond AI companies to mobile, automotive and networking customers.

The company said these agreements can support a more stable, contract-based business model. Samsung is moving toward a goal of allocating 60 to 70 percent of total production capacity to long-term contracts by 2030, according to the report.

Samsung has also received requests for additional supplies during existing contract periods and is reviewing its medium- to long-term production capabilities. With capacity already stretched, the company is considering how to meet additional demand without committing too quickly to expansion.

The market outlook is not without risks. New factories could lift DRAM supply significantly around 2028, while major technology companies face higher costs from AI investment and Chinese chipmakers are expanding capacity. Samsung plans to secure factory space first and install equipment in line with demand.

Samsung said higher capital spending in 2027 may not translate directly into higher chip output in 2028 because construction, equipment procurement and next-generation HBM manufacturing take time. For investors, the long-term agreements could improve revenue visibility, but the balance between secured demand, pricing and future capacity will remain important.
The broader market backdrop remains shaped by AI investment expectations and memory supply concerns. Current market reports provide further market context.

The slide in large-cap chip stocks follows a renewed flare-up of concerns over AI profitability in U.S. markets. On the 30th of last month, the Dow Jones industrial average and the S&P 500 closed down 1.09% and 1.82%, respectively, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.86%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 7.20%, with chip stocks broadly caught in the selloff, including Nvidia, down 4.22%, Broadcom, down 5.48%, and Micron, down 5.30%.

Earnings reports from Amazon and Intel ignited the concerns over AI profitability. Amazon posted third-quarter earnings per share of $1.89 and revenue of $201.94 billion, both below market estimates of $1.96 and $202.31 billion. Intel's third-quarter EPS and revenue beat expectations, but its fourth-quarter guidance for adjusted EPS of $0.25 and revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion fell short of the consensus of $0.43 and $17.1 billion. Analysts pointed to the burden of capital recovery and funding in the AI industry as a factor that could intensify downward pressure on equities going forward.

South Korea's Samsung Sells Out Initial Galaxy Buds On Stock in Three Days Despite approximately $220 Price Tag
sum: South Korea's Samsung Electronics has sold out the initial online inventory of its first clip-style wireless earbuds, the Galaxy Buds On, just three days after launch. Analysts say the open-ear design that leaves the ear canal unblocked has drawn demand from outdoor-activity users, even at the not-insignificant price of 299,000 won (approximately $220).

According to industry sources on November 1, the Galaxy Buds On, launched on October 27, ran through its initial stock at major online sales channels including Samsung.com, Coupang and Naver as of the afternoon of October 30. Those channels can no longer offer immediate shipment, and orders are available only as scheduled pre-orders. Samsung.com lists an estimated shipping start date of November 8.

South Korea is the first launch market for the Galaxy Buds On. In the U.S., sales begin in early November at $229. Samsung Electronics said it plans to roll the product out to other countries sequentially, but release dates and prices have not been disclosed for most regions, including Japan. The model number SM-U600 did, however, clear Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications technical conformity certification (giteki) on July 21, satisfying the wireless certification requirements for a local launch.

The core of the product is its wearing structure. It is the first in Samsung Electronics' Galaxy Buds lineup to adopt a clip-on design that hooks onto the outer ear rather than pushing into the ear canal. Because it does not fully block the ear, users can stay aware of their surroundings while listening to music, which is seen as making it well suited to outdoor activities such as running or walking.

The contact area uses a shape-memory alloy that conforms snugly to the user's ear shape and improves grip so the buds do not easily fall out during vigorous movement. Samsung Electronics said it analyzed ear data across various shapes and ran simulations to adjust the placement of the speakers and battery.
On the audio side, the buds pack TwinBoost speakers with enhanced bass and leakage-reduction technology that limits sound escaping outward.

sum: Samsung Electronics delays shareholder return details to Q1 next year
SK hynix launches 20 trillion won buyback to support share price floor

Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix — both of which posted record earnings for the third quarter — are facing a fresh test. Market attention has shifted away from the widely anticipated results and toward the sustainability of profit growth and the credibility of shareholder return plans. In the near term, the specificity and execution of those plans will be the key variable; over the medium to long term, the trajectory of AI infrastructure investment and its effect on memory demand and prices will determine where the stocks go.
Samsung Electronics opened Friday's Kospi session down 3.7 percent at 223,500 won ($167), while SK hynix fell 5.4 percent to open at 1.444 million won.

Samsung Electronics had already dropped 4.13 percent on Thursday after releasing its third-quarter results, and extended those losses at Friday's open. SK hynix, which disclosed its third-quarter earnings and an additional share buyback plan on Wednesday, gained 2.62 percent on Thursday, only to give back those gains at Friday's open.

The near-term variable for Samsung Electronics is the specificity of its shareholder return plan. The company said Thursday that total shareholder returns for this year would reach 90 trillion to 110 trillion won, but it did not disclose details on the remaining 55 trillion to 75 trillion won beyond the 35 trillion won already planned or distributed.

The company's decision to finalize the deployment plan for the remaining funds at a board meeting in January fell short of market expectations for more immediate shareholder return commitments. Hopes that Samsung Electronics would follow SK hynix with a concrete buyback plan — which would have drawn buying interest to support the share price floor — were dashed.

The Device Solutions (DS) division, which oversees the semiconductor business, recorded revenue of 147.1 trillion won and operating profit of 106.5 trillion won. In effect, the semiconductor division accounted for most of the company's total operating profit.

sum: Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (ISIN KR7005930003) is being valued at three times earnings in a report released October 26, 2026, as KB Securities argued that profit growth has outpaced the share price. The brokerage projected Samsung's operating profit at KRW 555 trillion for 2027, up 51 percent from a year earlier, according to Seoul Economic Daily.

The valuation argument arrives before Samsung's detailed third-quarter results. The company guided consolidated sales of KRW 195.00 trillion and operating profit of KRW 107.40 trillion on October 8, 2026, while giving ranges of KRW 194 trillion to KRW 196 trillion for sales and KRW 107.3 trillion to KRW 107.5 trillion for operating profit, according to Samsung Global Newsroom.

The guidance would mark a sharp acceleration from the second quarter of 2026, when revenue reached KRW 171.50 trillion and operating profit was KRW 89.49 trillion. CNBC reported that memory demand linked to artificial intelligence was the main driver of the improvement, while expectations for chip earnings had already become demanding.

The chronology is clear. On June 30, 2026, second-quarter revenue stood at KRW 171.50 trillion and operating profit at KRW 89.49 trillion, figures reported by CNBC. On October 8, 2026, Samsung guided third-quarter sales at KRW 195.00 trillion and operating profit at KRW 107.40 trillion, according to Samsung Global Newsroom. On October 26, 2026, KB Securities projected KRW 555 trillion in 2027 operating profit, according to Seoul Economic Daily.

Samsung's next substantiated date is October 29, 2026, when it has scheduled its third-quarter earnings conference call at 10:00 a.m. Korea Standard Time. The investor-relations calendar also identifies October 8, 2026, as the date of the third-quarter guidance announcement, according to Samsung Electronics.

For investors, the key test is whether the projected profit expansion becomes visible in the final business-unit breakdown. KB Securities said Samsung's earnings growth and share price had diverged, while the October 29 report should provide a more detailed view of memory profitability and shareholder returns.

sum: Asset disclosure of former North Pyongan Province Governor Lee Se-ung
Stock portfolio surged on back of 840,000-plus Samsung Electronics shares

Lee Se-ung, former governor of North Pyongan Province under the Ministry of Interior and Safety's Five Northern Provinces Committee — a vice-ministerial-level post — saw his declared assets grow by 117.23 billion won ($88.5 million) in seven months, driven almost entirely by a surge in the value of his stock holdings, including 840,000 shares of Samsung Electronics.

The Government Ethics Committee published senior officials' asset registrations in the official gazette Friday. Lee reported combined assets of 275.95 billion won in his own and his spouse's names upon leaving office. The registration date was July 21, shortly after his retirement.
That figure is 2.25 times the 122.46 billion won he declared when he was first appointed governor of North Pyongan Province in August 2024 — a more than doubling in roughly two years.

Compared with the 158.72 billion won he reported at the end of last year and made public in March, his assets rose by 117.23 billion won, or 73.9 percent. Both the total and the increase ranked first among the 82 officials covered in this disclosure round.
A breakdown of Lee's filing shows that the bulk of the increase came from a rise in the assessed value of his listed stock holdings.

Samsung Preferred Shares Gain on Buyback Hopes, Narrowing Gap With Common Stock
sum: - Samsung Electronics’ large-scale shareholder return plan and expectations for share buybacks are raising the likelihood that the price gap will narrow between undervalued preferred shares and common stock.

- The market is focused on the view that buying back and retiring preferred shares, which trade at a deeper discount than common stock, would allow a company to cancel more shares with the same amount of money and reduce future dividend costs.

- In South Korea, preferred shares issued by many companies including Hyundai Motor trade at an average 45% discount to common stock, raising expectations that expanded buybacks and cancellations of preferred shares could help ease the Korea discount.

Samsung Electronics Co.’s sweeping shareholder return plan is fueling expectations that its undervalued preferred shares could be included in future buybacks, raising the prospect that the price gap with its common stock will narrow.

Bloomberg reported on September 7 that market participants see Samsung as potentially favoring preferred shares over common stock in future repurchases because they trade at a steeper discount. Samsung preferred shares currently trade about 26% below the common stock. The gap has narrowed from 37% on recent buyback expectations, but it remains near the widest level in more than a decade.

Last month, Samsung announced a shareholder return plan worth as much as 110 trillion won ($81.2 billion) to share with investors profits from growth in its artificial intelligence business. The company did not disclose a specific buyback amount. Investors are focused on the fact that buying back and retiring lower-priced preferred shares would allow Samsung to cancel more stock with the same amount of money while also reducing future dividend costs.

Governance considerations are also driving expectations for preferred-share buybacks. Under South Korean law, Samsung’s financial affiliates face restrictions on holding voting common shares in Samsung Electronics above a certain level. If Samsung were to buy back and retire a large amount of common stock, those affiliates’ ownership stakes could rise and potentially force them to sell some shares. Repurchasing non-voting preferred shares would avoid that burden.

sum: This week (the 7th–11th), Korea's stock market is expected to be heavily influenced by whether U.S. Government Bonds yields stabilize. As the U.S. Treasury expands the size of its long-term bond buyback, inflation indicators that will shape the Federal Reserve's policy rate path will also be released in succession.

On Aug. 31–Sept. 4, Korea's stock market weakened on unstable macroeconomic variables. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix continued to buy back their own shares, but rising U.S. Government Bonds yields and tensions in the Middle East weighed on the market.

With the United States resuming airstrikes on Iran for the first time in a month and pushing international oil prices above $90 per barrel, inflation concerns have flared again. In response, the U.S. 10-year Government Bonds yield rose to as high as 4.8%, the highest since Jan. 2025, adding pressure to Korea's stock market.

However, ahead of the weekend, dovish (favoring monetary easing) remarks by senior Federal Reserve officials partially eased the burden of high rates. Christopher Waller, a Federal Reserve governor, noted that if upcoming inflation data confirm easing price pressures, he would be inclined to support holding the policy rate steady.
According to the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) FedWatch, the chance of the Fed holding rates in September rose to 49.5% on the 3rd from 36.8% on the 2nd.

Market focus this week is also expected to converge on the U.S. rate trajectory. Lee Jae-won of Yuanta Securities Korea said, "A slowdown in jobs and price indicators, along with the Treasury's efforts to stabilize long-term bond supply and demand, are factors that could lower rates."

First, on the 9th, the U.S. Treasury will expand the size of its long-term Government Bonds buyback. The per-operation purchase size will be increased from $2 billion to $4 billion. When the Treasury buys long-term Government Bonds, the amount of long-dated paper circulating in the market decreases, which can drive up Government Bonds prices and push down long-term yields.

sum: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix's massive share buyback programs have translated into aggressive net buying by "other corporations" in the South Korean stock market, emerging as a core pillar of market supply and demand. Yet even after the two companies purchased more than ₩10 trillion worth of their own shares in just over a week, the KOSPI remains unable to muster momentum at the 7,000 threshold.

According to the Korea Exchange and financial data provider Yonhap Infomax on the 28th, other corporations recorded net purchases exceeding ₩1 trillion per day for seven consecutive trading sessions from the 20th through the close of trading that day. Cumulative net buying on the KOSPI during this period reached ₩10.19 trillion (approximately $7.4 billion). On the day itself, they added another ₩1.06 trillion (approximately $774.2 million) in the final ten minutes before the market close.

The shift in buying scale is dramatic compared with early-to-mid August. From the 1st through the 19th of this month, other corporations' average daily net purchases amounted to just ₩18.7 billion (approximately $13.6 million). The figure surged starting on the 20th, when Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix's buyback programs kicked into full gear.

By individual stock, other corporations net purchased ₩2.47 trillion (approximately $1.8 billion) of Samsung Electronics and ₩7.62 trillion (approximately $5.6 billion) of SK Hynix during this period. In contrast, foreign investors, retail investors, and pension funds were largely net sellers of both stocks. Foreign and retail investors net sold ₩5.91 trillion (approximately $4.3 billion) and ₩3.22 trillion (approximately $2.3 billion) respectively on the KOSPI over the same period.

Samsung Electronics disclosed on the 21st that it would purchase approximately ₩15 trillion (approximately $10.9 billion) worth of treasury shares on the open market from the 24th through November 21 for the purpose of employee stock compensation. SK Hynix is acquiring ₩40 trillion (approximately $29.2 billion) in treasury shares on the open market from the 20th of this month through November 19.

The KOSPI was trading at 6,899.50 as of 2:41 p.m. local time, up 1.34%, or 91.29 points, for the session. The gain came after a much stronger open, with the index jumping 2.76% at the start of trading to 6,996.12, before some of those gains were pared back through the day.

The rally traces directly back to Nvidia's quarterly report, released after the U.S. market close Wednesday. The chip giant beat Wall Street's revenue and earnings expectations and signaled that shortages in advanced memory chips are likely to persist through fiscal 2028, a forecast that reinforced investor confidence in the artificial intelligence spending cycle that has powered much of this year's rally in Korean tech stocks.

Analysts had been watching the report closely, given how tightly Korea's two largest chipmakers are woven into Nvidia's supply chain. Nvidia's high-bandwidth memory order guidance was seen as a direct signal for the forward trajectories of both SK Hynix and Samsung, and Nvidia's commentary on chip demand carried outsized weight for a market that has already priced in years of rapid growth.

Domestic chip bellwethers powered Thursday's advance. Samsung Electronics traded at 270,000 won early in the session, up 3.25%, while SK Hynix rose 5.45% to 1.78 million won, according to Korea Exchange data. The buying spread across the broader semiconductor supply chain, lifting shares of SK Square, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Hanmi Semiconductor as well.

SK Hynix also had company-specific news working in its favor. The chipmaker said Wednesday it plans to invest 21.6 trillion won, or roughly $15.07 billion, to build a new production facility in Yongin, and separately announced a partnership with SanDisk Corp. to develop high-bandwidth flash memory, which the company described as a next-generation storage architecture that will be central to future AI development.

sum: On July 21, Samsung Electronics established the RX (Robotics eXperience) division, reporting directly to the CEO to accelerate robotics commercialization. By integrating R&D with its AI, hardware, and global sales ecosystem, Samsung aims to deploy robotics across manufacturing, logistics, and home services. While the move signals a transition toward independent operations, near-term revenue impact remains limited. Following the announcement, stock prices rose over 5% as markets welcomed the strategic diversification. However, long-term valuation depends on successful product launches and achieving profitability, as the business currently remains in a capital-intensive investment phase.

TradingKey - On July 21, Samsung Electronics announced the establishment of RX, its robotics business division, fully named "Robotics eXperience." The new division will report directly to the company's CEO and will be responsible for formulating mid-to-long-term robotics business strategies, researching and developing core technologies, and promoting product commercialization, while expanding Samsung's robotics R&D capabilities in South Korea and overseas.

This organizational adjustment shows that Samsung is pushing its robotics business further from the technology R&D stage toward independent operations and commercial implementation. As early as 2025, Samsung established the Future Robotics Office reporting directly to the CEO and increased its stake in South Korean robotics company Rainbow Robotics to 35%, becoming its largest shareholder. The two parties plan to combine Samsung's strengths in artificial intelligence, software, and global sales channels with Rainbow Robotics' technology in humanoid and collaborative robots to accelerate the development of advanced robots.

In terms of application scenarios, Samsung's robotics business is expected to cover fields such as smart manufacturing, logistics and transportation, industrial inspection, and home services. The company previously proposed to transform its global manufacturing bases into "AI-driven factories" by 2030, and gradually introduce humanoid, logistics, and assembly robots to enhance production efficiency, safety, and automation.

The KOSPI index fell over 6% at one point during the session, prompting the Korea Exchange to urgently trigger a program trading circuit breaker, suspending program trading sell orders for 5 minutes.

However, selling pressure on Korean stocks remained unabated in the afternoon. As of press time, the KOSPI index was down 5.87%, temporarily trading at 7816.39 points. The KOSPI index opened lower and trended downward today, but later rebounded, briefly rising above the 8,000-point mark during the session.

In terms of individual stocks, the two memory giants performed largely in line with the broader market but suffered larger declines. Samsung Electronics plunged 7.15%, once again testing the 290,000 won threshold, temporarily trading at 292,000 won and touching its June 11 low; SK Hynix fell 8.83%, temporarily trading at 2,334,000 won and hitting its June 17 low.

sum: Japanese and South Korean equity markets declined sharply on June 26, with the Nikkei 225 and KOSPI both dropping approximately 3%. Semiconductor leaders, including Kioxia, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics, faced significant selling pressure. The downturn reflects investor anxiety over U.S. inflationary trends, following a 4.1% rise in May PCE data, which fuels expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Additionally, unresolved geopolitical tensions concerning energy shipping routes continue to weigh on market sentiment in these import-dependent economies, curbing risk appetite and triggering a broad pullback in tech-heavy indices.

TradingKey - Japanese and South Korean stock markets opened lower and continued to fall, with the KOSPI and Nikkei 225 indices dropping by about 3%, while Kioxia, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics plummeted in tandem.

During the Asian trading session on June 26, Japanese and South Korean stock markets opened lower and slid further. Specifically, South Korea's KOSPI index fell over 2.97%, dropping 265 points to temporarily stand at 8,664.71 points; the Nikkei 225 retreated 2.94%, falling more than 2,000 points to temporarily trade at 70,240.09 points.

In terms of individual stocks, Kioxia fell 3.13%, retreating to around 100,000 yen, temporarily trading at 100,650 yen; SK Hynix fell 1.58%, slipping below the 2.9 million won threshold, temporarily trading at 2,871,000 won; Samsung Electronics fell 1.53%, temporarily trading at 353,000 won.

Although Micron Technology ( MU )'s strong earnings report briefly stimulated Asian semiconductor stocks, the U.S. May PCE rose 4.1% year-over-year, hitting a near three-year high and boosting expectations for Federal Reserve rate hikes this year. Overnight, the overall trend of U.S. stocks was not optimistic, with tech giants generally pulling back, as heavyweight stocks like Microsoft ( MSFT ), Apple ( AAPL) and other heavyweight stocks collectively moved lower, dragging down the Nasdaq Index to a lower close.

In addition, although recent reports indicated that the U.S. and Iran were expected to reach an agreement and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, prompting oil prices to retreat, the latest geopolitical details show that the core conflicts between the two sides have not been fully resolved.
